propositions.text: The Appellant, a Pakistani citizen, appeals the RPD decision rejecting his refugee claim.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant), a citizen of Pakistan, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection.

propositions.text: The Appellant asks the RAD to set aside the RPD decision and find him a Convention refugee or person in need of protection.
propositions.quote: The Appellant asks that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) set aside the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) and substitute a decision with its own determination that the Appellant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection.

propositions.text: Alternatively, the Appellant requests the RAD refer the matter back to the RPD with a differently constituted panel.
propositions.quote: In the alternative, the Appellant requests that the RAD refer the matter back to the RPD with a differently constituted panel.

propositions.text: The Appellant submitted new evidence under section 110(4) IRPA and requests an oral hearing under section 110(6) IRPA.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has submitted new evidence with the appeal as referred to in Section 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA)1 and requests an oral hearing be held pursuant to Section 110(6) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Appellant, a Pakistani citizen, appeals the RPD decision and requests the RAD set aside or refer back the decision, submitting new evidence and requesting an oral hearing.

propositions.text: The RAD confirms the RPD decision and dismisses the appeal under section 111(1)(a) IRPA.
propositions.quote: Pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, the RAD confirms the determination of the RPD and dismisses the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD confirms the RPD decision and dismisses the appeal under section 111(1)(a) IRPA, the court states.

propositions.text: The Appellant fears the Taliban due to his tribal affiliation and anti-Taliban political opinion.
propositions.quote: The Appellant alleged before the RPD that he fears the Tehrik-e-Taliban ("TTP" or "Taliban") if he were to return to Pakistan due to his tribal affiliation and anti-Taliban political opinion.

propositions.text: His tribe formed a group of about XXXX people to monitor the Taliban and report to the government.
propositions.quote: The Appellant alleges his tribe formed a XXXX XXXX XXXX consisting of about XXXX XXXX people to monitor the Taliban and report back to the government.

propositions.text: The Appellant was a leader of about XXXX men in that group.
propositions.quote: The Appellant alleges he was a XXXX XXXX XXXX of about XXXX men in the XXXX XXXX XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant alleges before the RPD he fears the Taliban due to tribal affiliation and political opinion, and was a leader in a tribal group monitoring the Taliban.

propositions.text: In 2011, Taliban left pamphlets demanding he stop his activities.
propositions.quote: In 2011, the Appellant alleges the Taliban left pamphlets in front of his house demanding he stop his activities on the XXXX XXXX.

propositions.text: In 2012, his family returned home but a group demanded protection money and beat him twice for resisting.
propositions.quote: In 2012 the Appellant and his family returned to their home in the village of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX However the area was controlled by the group XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX who demanded protection money from the Appellant to protect them from the Taliban. The Appellant alleges he was beaten twice by this group for resisting to pay the protection money.

propositions.text: In 2013, fighting between Taliban and the group caused him to flee, then return, then move family to another area due to Taliban searching for him.
propositions.quote: In XXXX of 2013 there was intense fighting between the Taliban and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. He and his family fled their homes and went to the XXXX area. Subsequently, they went back to XXXX. The Taliban came looking for him and he decided to move his family to the XXXX area of XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant alleges Taliban threatened him in 2011, he was beaten by another group in 2012, and fled fighting in 2013, moving family due to Taliban search.

propositions.text: In 2014, the Appellant left Pakistan with an agent, traveled through countries, entered US, detained over one year, asylum claim refused in 2015, then claimed refugee in Canada in 2016.
propositions.quote: On XXXX XXXX, 2014 the Appellant left Pakistan with the assistance of an agent, travelling through several countries before entering the United States (US) on XXXX XXXX, 2014 where he was detained for over one year. He made an asylum claim in the US which was refused in XXXX of 2015. On XXXX XXXX, 2016 the Appellant made a refugee claim at the port of entry in XXXX, Manitoba.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant left Pakistan in 2014, was detained in the US, had asylum refused, then claimed refugee status in Canada in 2016, he says.

propositions.text: The RPD rejected the Appellant's claim in 2016, finding him not credible.
propositions.quote: In a decision of November 10, 2016, the RPD rejected the Appellant's claim finding that the Appellant was not credible.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits the RPD erred in credibility findings and treatment of documentary evidence.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that the RPD erred in drawing its credibility findings and in its treatment of the documentary evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD rejected the Appellant's claim as not credible; the Appellant argues the RPD erred in credibility and evidence treatment.

propositions.text: The RAD finds the Federal Court of Appeal decision in Huruglica guides the standard of review for specialized tribunals like the RAD.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the Federal Court of Appeal decision, in Huruglica,2 provides the RAD with guidance in relation to the appropriate standard that must be applied by a specialized tribunal, such as the RAD, to decisions of a first-level administrative tribunal.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds Huruglica guides the standard of review for specialized tribunals reviewing first-level administrative decisions.

propositions.text: The RAD reviews RPD findings of fact and mixed fact and law on correctness standard, conducting its own analysis.
propositions.quote: The RAD concludes from its statutory analysis that, with respect to findings of fact (and mixed fact and law), the RAD is to review RPD decisions applying the correctness standard.

propositions.text: The RAD carefully considers the RPD decision and analyzes the record to determine if the RPD erred as submitted by the Appellant.
propositions.quote: Thus, after carefully considering the RPD's decision, the RAD carries out its own analysis of the record to determine whether, as submitted by the Appellant, the RPD erred.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD applies correctness standard to RPD fact findings and conducts its own analysis to determine if RPD erred, the court states.

propositions.text: Section 110(3) IRPA requires RAD to proceed without hearing on RPD record, accepting documentary evidence and written submissions.
propositions.quote: As provided for in s. 110(3) of the IRPA, with certain exceptions, the RAD must proceed without a hearing, on the basis of the record of the proceedings of the RPD and may accept documentary evidence and written submissions from the Minister and refugee claimant.

propositions.text: Section 110(4) IRPA allows appeal evidence only if it arose after rejection, was not reasonably available, or could not reasonably have been presented before rejection.
propositions.quote: Section 110(4) of the IRPA provides that the person who is the subject of the appeal may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD must proceed without hearing on RPD record but may accept new evidence only if it arose after rejection or was not reasonably available before, court explains.

propositions.text: The Appellant submitted three news articles as new evidence with the appeal record.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has submitted three news articles3 as proposed new evidence with the Appellant's Record.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant submitted three news articles as new evidence with the appeal record, the court notes.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits the new evidence meets section 110(4) IRPA test as it arose after the refugee claim rejection.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submit that the proposed new evidence meets the test of s. 110(4) of the IRPA because it arose after the refugee claims.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant submits the new evidence meets section 110(4) IRPA test as it arose after claim rejection, he argues.

propositions.text: The RAD agrees further analysis is needed before accepting new evidence but finds Raza analysis not fully appropriate for RAD evidence assessment.
propositions.quote: While the RAD agrees with the Appellant that further analysis of the evidence is required before the RAD can accept the proposed new evidence, the analysis as set out in Raza4 is not entirely appropriate for the purpose of assessing evidence submitted to the RAD.

propositions.text: The RAD is guided by the Federal Court of Appeal decision in Singh for assessing evidence submitted to the RAD.
propositions.quote: In this regard, the RAD is guided by the Federal Court of Appeal decision in Singh.5

paragraphs.summary: The RAD agrees further analysis is needed before accepting new evidence and is guided by Singh, finding Raza analysis not fully appropriate.

propositions.text: The RAD has adapted the Raza analysis to assess evidence submitted to the RAD.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, the RAD has adapted the analysis in Raza6 to the assessment of evidence submitted to the RAD.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD has adapted the Raza analysis to assess evidence submitted to the RAD, the court states.

propositions.text: The RAD considers seven factors in assessing if new evidence meets section 110(4) IRPA requirements.
propositions.quote: In assessing whether the proposed new evidence meets the statutory provisions of s. 110(4), the RAD considered the following: a) First, did the evidence arise after the rejection of the Appellant's refugee claim?... g) If the proposed new evidence meets the tests set out in the statutory requirements and in Raza,13 the evidence will be admitted as evidence in the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD considers multiple factors to assess if new evidence meets section 110(4) IRPA requirements, including timing, availability, and relevance.

propositions.text: The Appellant submitted three news articles published in December 2016 as new evidence.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has submitted three news articles as new evidence in this appeal. a. An article from DAWN.com, "Five Terrorists Shot Dead in Encounter", published December 19, 201614 b. An article from TNN.com, "Waquas trained in Taliban jihad camps", published December 15, 2016.15 c. An article published in the Nation newspaper, "ISIS men among 7 held in Multan, Sialkot raids", published December 14, 2016.16

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant submitted three news articles published in December 2016 as new evidence, the court notes.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits the articles arose after claim rejection and are relevant to terrorism in proposed IFA locations.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits the articles were all published since the rejection of his refugee claim and that they are all relevant in that they reference terrorism related activity in the proposed IFA location of Lahore, Hyderabad or Multan.

propositions.text: The RAD finds the articles meet section 110(4) IRPA as they arose after claim rejection and meet Raza requirements as new and relevant evidence.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds these documents meet the basic requirement of section 110(4) as they all arose following the rejection of the Appellant's claim for refugee protection. The RAD further finds the articles do meet the requirements of Raza.17 , in that they are new and they do address terrorist activities in the proposed IFA location.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant submits the articles arose after claim rejection and are relevant; the RAD finds they meet section 110(4) and Raza requirements.

propositions.text: The RAD admits the three news articles as new evidence in the appeal.
propositions.quote: The RAD will admit these documents as new evidence in this appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD admits the three news articles as new evidence in the appeal, the court orders.

propositions.text: Section 110(6) IRPA allows RAD to hold a hearing if new documentary evidence raises a serious credibility issue central to the RPD decision that could justify claim allowance or rejection.
propositions.quote: According to Section 110(6), upon which the Appellant relies, the RAD may hold a hearing if, in its opinion, there is documentary evidence referred to in 110(3) that raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the Appellant, that is central to the RPD's decision, and that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.

propositions.text: In this appeal, with no Minister evidence, documentary evidence under 110(3) must be understood in relation to 110(4).
propositions.quote: In this appeal, where there is no evidence from or in response to the Minister, the documentary evidence referred to in Section 110(3) must be understood in relation to Section 110(4).

paragraphs.summary: The RAD explains section 110(6) allows a hearing if new evidence raises serious credibility issues central to the RPD decision; here, evidence under 110(3) relates to 110(4).

propositions.text: Sections 110(3), (4), and (6) together require the RAD not to hold a hearing unless new evidence raises a serious credibility issue central to the RPD decision that could justify claim allowance or rejection.
propositions.quote: When read together, Sections 110(3), (4), and (6) establish that the RAD must not hold a hearing in an appeal such as this unless there is new (Section 110(4)) evidence, in which case the RAD may hold a hearing if that new evidence raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the Appellant, is central to the RPD's decision, and that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD states it must not hold a hearing unless new evidence raises serious credibility issues central to the RPD decision that could justify claim allowance or rejection.

propositions.text: Article a shows police killed five suspected TTP terrorists in Lahore, indicating Taliban presence but active police counteraction; no evidence Taliban can locate Appellant in IFA location.
propositions.quote: Article "a", "Five Terrorists Shot Dead in Encounter", details that the Counter Terrorism Department (CTD) of the police in Lahore killed five suspected terrorists belonging to the TTP. The article further noted that the police recovered a number of weapons and they continue to pursue three or four accomplices who escaped. The Appellant submits that the article supports the notion that Taliban terrorists are active in Lahore. The RAD notes that while the article indicates that a Taliban faction may be present in Lahore, it confirms that the police in Lahore are taking an active role in attempting to counteract and subdue terrorist activities, and they were successful in this instance. The RAD further finds that the article does not provide any evidence to support the appellant's argument that the Taliban have the ability to locate him in the proposed IFA location. The RAD finds it does not provide persuasive evidence to support this central element of the Appellant's claim.

propositions.text: Article b describes conviction of a man with Taliban ties in Hyderabad but no evidence they are Taliban members or communicate with Taliban; authorities successfully arrested terrorists; article does not justify claim allowance or rejection.
propositions.quote: Article "b", "Waquas trained in Taliban jihad camps", describes that a highly sought individual, was tried along with four others and convicted of a 2013, bombing of a shopping district in Hyderabad. The appellant submits that the conviction of a man with ties to the Taliban is relevant to his argument that Hyderabad is not safe as a potential IFA location. The RAD notes that the article does not state that these individuals are members of the Taliban. The RAD additionally notes that there is no persuasive evidence to support the concept that these individuals had any ability to communicate directly with the Taliban. The RAD further finds that the article confirms a successful arrest and prosecution of a wanted terrorist by the authorities in Pakistan. The RAD finds this article does not provide evidence that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.

propositions.text: Article c reports arrests of terrorists including ISIS and TTP members plotting attacks in Multan; Taliban traveled there to attack; attacks are general, not targeted at individuals; any Pakistani citizen could be at risk.
propositions.quote: Article "c", "ISIS men among 7 held in Multan, Sialkot raids", details that the provincial CTD arrested seven terrorists, in two separate investigations, three of whom were alleged to be members of ISIS. The article notes the militants were plotting gun and bomb attacks on shrines, religious processions and government installations. The article carries on to describe a second arrest of four individuals who were associated with the TTP, who had come to Multan to launch attacks on sensitive installations and law enforcement. The RAD notes the article does not indicate the Taliban are active in Multan, but it clearly states the Taliban members traveled to Multan to carry out their attack. The RAD additionally notes that the terrorist attacks described in this article are not targeted at a single individual, but appear to be designed to focus on disruptive techniques inflicting harm on any or all who may be present in the immediate area. The RAD finds that any Pakistani citizen could be at risk of thi

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the three articles show Taliban presence and arrests but do not support the Appellant's claim that Taliban can locate or target him specifically in proposed IFA locations.

propositions.text: New evidence admitted but insufficient to support Taliban seeking appellant in IFA location
propositions.quote: The RAD finds the documents provide insufficient persuasive evidence to support the Appellant's allegation that the Taliban in Pakistan will be able to seek him out in the IFA location.

propositions.text: Evidence shows Pakistani authorities actively counter terrorist groups
propositions.quote: At its best they establish that the authorities in Pakistan are actively attempting to detect and counteract the efforts of terrorist groups.

propositions.text: Evidence lacks materiality to justify allowing or rejecting refugee claim under s.110(6)
propositions.quote: Accordingly the evidence lacks the materiality to justify either allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim, and, as such, it does not meet the requirements of 110(6).

propositions.text: All requirements of s.110(6)(a)-(c) must be met; here (b) and (c) are not met
propositions.quote: Each of the requirements in 110(6)(a) through (c) have to be met, and in this case the requirement in 110(6)(b and c) are not met.

propositions.text: No discretion to hold a hearing under s.110(6)
propositions.quote: As such, the RAD has no discretion to hold a hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds new evidence insufficient to show Taliban can find appellant in IFA; s.110(6)(b) and (c) unmet; no hearing discretion.

propositions.text: RAD must proceed without hearing on RPD record; oral hearing denied
propositions.quote: As such, the RAD must proceed without a hearing on the basis of the RPD's record, and his application for an oral hearing is denied.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD denies oral hearing and proceeds on RPD record without hearing.

propositions.text: RPD failed to consider psychotherapist report diagnosing appellant with anxiety disorder and other conditions
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that the RPD failed to take into consideration the findings of the "XXXXt" that the Appellant suffers from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX anxiety disorder and a XXXX XXXX XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the RPD ignored a psychotherapist report diagnosing anxiety and other disorders.

propositions.text: RPD considered Ms. XXXX's report; RAD conducted own assessment
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the RPD considered the report of Ms. XXXX. Notwithstanding the foregoing, the RAD has conducted its own assessment the XXXXreport18.

propositions.text: Ms. XXXX is a registered psychotherapist, not a medical doctor, psychiatrist, or psychologist
propositions.quote: the RAD notes that report's author, Ms. XXXX is not a medical doctor, psychiatrist, or psychologist. Rather, she is a registered XXXX "specializing in the assessment and treatment of serious disorders of thought, cognition, mood, emotional regulation, perception, and memory."

propositions.text: Ms. XXXX's assessments are based on in-depth clinical and psychodynamic interviews
propositions.quote: Her assessments are based on "in-depth clinical and psychodynamic interviews, typically extending for 60 minutes."19

paragraphs.summary: The RAD notes RPD considered Ms. XXXX's report; Ms. XXXX is a psychotherapist, not a doctor or psychologist, using clinical interviews.

propositions.text: Ms. XXXX appears to communicate a diagnosis consistent with appellant's symptoms
propositions.quote: she appears to communicate a diagnosis finding that the Appellant is exhibiting symptoms consistent with XXXX as well as XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.

propositions.text: Section 27 of Regulated Health Professionals Act restricts who may communicate diagnoses
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that section 27 of the Regulated Health Professionals Act, S.O. 1991, Chapter 18 describes the communication of a diagnosis as a "controlled act," not to be performed unless the communicator is so authorized by a health profession Act, or unless the action has been delegated by a person who is so authorized.

propositions.text: Ms. XXXX does not appear authorized to communicate diagnosis under the Act
propositions.quote: It does not appear that Ms. XXXX meets either qualification.

propositions.text: Controlled act of diagnosis involves communicating disease or disorder causing symptoms where reliance is foreseeable
propositions.quote: The controlled act of diagnosis, at S.27(2)(1), is communicating to the individual or his personal representative a diagnosis identifying a disease or disorder as the cause of symptoms of the individual in circumstances in which it is reasonably foreseeable that the individual or his personal representative will rely on the diagnosis.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds Ms. XXXX communicated a diagnosis without authorization, contrary to the Regulated Health Professionals Act.

propositions.text: Ms. XXXX's letter communicates a diagnosis to be relied on in proceedings
propositions.quote: Ms. XXXX letter clearly sets out to communicate a diagnosis, to be relied upon in these proceedings.

propositions.text: Contravention of Regulated Health Professionals Act by psychotherapist is professional misconduct
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that contravention of the Regulated Health Professionals Act by a psychotherapist is considered professional misconduct.20

propositions.text: Report deserves little weight as author is unqualified to diagnose
propositions.quote: This assessment deserves little weight, as its author is neither a doctor nor a psychologist and therefore not qualified to make or communicate a diagnosis.21

propositions.text: No evidence any medical or therapeutic care plan was implemented
propositions.quote: there is no evidence that any such plan was put in place.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds Ms. XXXX's diagnosis communication is professional misconduct and gives the report little weight; no care plan shown.

propositions.text: Ms. XXXX advocated for appellant to remain in Canada beyond report scope
propositions.quote: Ms. XXXX went well beyond the scope of even a psychological or psychiatric report when she went on to advocate for the Appellant to remain in Canada.

propositions.text: RAD gives no weight to Ms. XXXX's report
propositions.quote: For all these reasons, the RAD gives this report no weight.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds Ms. XXXX improperly advocated for appellant and gives her report no weight.

propositions.text: Determinative issue is Internal Flight Alternative (IFA); RPD found appellant has reasonable IFA in Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore
propositions.quote: The RAD finds, after its own review and assessment of the evidence, that the determinative issue in this appeal is IFA. The RPD found that the Appellant has a reasonable IFA in Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds IFA is the key issue; RPD found appellant has reasonable IFA in three cities.

propositions.text: RPD's IFA assessment disregards documentary evidence in NDP and post-hearing submissions
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that the RPD assessment of his IFA is based in disregard for the documentary evidence provided in the National Documentation Package (NDP) and post-hearing submissions.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the RPD ignored documentary evidence in assessing IFA.

propositions.text: IFA test from Rasaratnam has two prongs: no serious persecution risk and reasonable to seek refuge there
propositions.quote: In assessing an IFA, the RAD must apply a two-pronged test cited in Rasaratnam:22 1) the Board must be satisfied on a balance of probabilities that there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted in the part of the country to which it finds an IFA exists and/or the claimant would not be personally subject to a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture in the IFA. 2) moreover, the conditions in the part of the country considered to be an IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable, in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claim, for the claimant to seek refuge there.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD states the two-pronged Rasaratnam test for IFA: no serious persecution risk and reasonable to seek refuge there.

propositions.text: Both prongs must be met to find IFA; burden on appellant to disprove IFA; IFA must be realistic and safe
propositions.quote: Both prongs must be satisfied to find that the Appellant has an IFA. The burden of proof rests with the Appellant to show that he does not have an IFA. The finding of an IFA must be based on a distinct evaluation of a region for that purpose taking into account the Appellant's identity. An IFA must be a realistic and attainable option. The Appellant cannot be required to encounter great physical danger or to undergo undue hardship in traveling there or staying there.23

paragraphs.summary: The RAD explains burden on appellant to disprove IFA; IFA must be realistic and safe.

propositions.text: TTP is an alliance of militant groups, not a unified organization
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that the documentary evidence indicates the TTP in Pakistan does not operate as a unified, integrated organization with a solitary hierarchical structure.

propositions.text: IRB research directorate July 2014 describes TTP as alliance of militant groups with loose factions
propositions.quote: Sources describe Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) ... as "an alliance of militant groups" ... "a coalition" ... "an umbrella organization" ... not a unified fighting force ... control different regions ... factions don't always speak with one voice" (CNN 17 Oct. 2012).

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds TTP is a fractious alliance of militant groups without unified structure, per IRB July 2014.

propositions.text: TTP can deploy suicide bombers and is a threat throughout Pakistan
propositions.quote: The RAD further notes that the documentation states that "their ability to deploy suicide bombers makes them a threat throughout Pakistan".

propositions.text: No indication TTP targets specific individuals unless high profile
propositions.quote: it does not indicate that a specific individual would be targeted if they are not a high profile person.

propositions.text: Appellant was not high profile and lived in Peshawar area without Taliban problems
propositions.quote: The RAD notes the Appellant has testified that he was a member of the peace committee where he lived... appellant did not occupy a high profile position... appellant's ability to reside in the XXXX area of Peshawar for three to four months without any problems with the Taliban.

propositions.text: Highly unlikely appellant would be personally targeted by Taliban in other areas
propositions.quote: Therefore, the RAD finds the Appellant's it highly unlikely the Appellant would be personally targeted by the Taliban in other areas in Pakistan.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds TTP is a threat but unlikely to target appellant personally given his low profile and residence in Peshawar.

propositions.text: UK Home Office cites Australian DFAT Nov 2013 assessment on internal relocation in Pakistan
propositions.quote: Country documentation from the United Kingdom Home Office states: The Australian Government Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) provided an assessment, published November 2013, with regard to internal relocation in Pakistan...

propositions.text: Internal relocation offers anonymity and refuge from discrimination or violence in Pakistan's large urban centers
propositions.quote: 'Because of Pakistan's size and diversity, internal relocation offers a degree of anonymity and the opportunity for victims to seek refuge from discrimination or violence... many large urban centres are home to mixed ethnic and religious communities and offer greater opportunities for employment, access to services and a greater degree of state protection than other areas.'

propositions.text: Internal relocation limited by financial resources and debts to landowners or money lenders
propositions.quote: internal relocation is most successful when these conditions exist, but is limited mostly by a lack of financial resources and in some cases due to debts owed to landowners or money lenders.'

paragraphs.summary: The RAD cites UK Home Office and Australian DFAT that internal relocation in Pakistan offers anonymity and refuge in large cities, limited by finances.

propositions.text: UNHCR Guidelines state viable IFA unavailable for those targeted by armed militant groups with wide reach
propositions.quote: Given the wide geographic reach of some armed militant groups, a viable IFA will generally not be available to individuals at risk of being targeted by such groups.

propositions.text: Certain militant groups have operational capacity beyond FATA or Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, with high-profile attacks countrywide
propositions.quote: The operational capacity of certain militant groups, such as the Lashkar-e-Jhangvi and Sipah-e-Sahaba Pakistan, extends far beyond FATA or the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province as evidenced by high-profile attacks, such as suicide bombings, countrywide, particularly in urban centres.

propositions.text: Non-State agents of persecution often linked to local and central authorities, operating with impunity beyond immediate control areas
propositions.quote: some non-State agents of persecution... reportedly have links to or are closely associated with influential actors in the local and central administration, law enforcement and/or judiciary... often operate with impunity and their reach may extend beyond the area(s) under their immediate control.

paragraphs.summary: UNHCR Guidelines say some militant groups have wide reach and impunity, limiting viable IFA for targeted individuals.

propositions.text: UNHCR document states some militant groups have reach beyond origin areas, but does not reference TTP
propositions.quote: The RAD has considered the statements in the UNHCR document which clearly states certain militant groups... have a reach beyond their physical point of origin. The RAD has considered that the IRB Response to Information Request (RIR) discussed previously specifically notes that the TTP are a fractious group and they do not appear to have the ability to track individuals.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD notes UNHCR says some militant groups have wide reach but TTP is fractious and lacks tracking ability.

propositions.text: RPD found no evidence TTP in Peshawar region would learn appellant's presence in Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that the RPD found that there was no documentary evidence to support that the TTP members in XXXX, (Peshawar region) who targeted the Appellant would learn of the Appellant's presence in Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore.

propositions.text: Evidence shows TTP is not unified and has limited activity in Lahore; security situation in Lahore and Islamabad relatively free from terrorist violence
propositions.quote: The evidence before the RPD and the RAD establishes the TTP in Pakistan does not operate as a unified, integrated organization... British Home Office references an Australian government source saying that 'the current security situation in Islamabad and Lahore is relatively free from politically-motivated, terrorist and sectarian violence.'

propositions.text: Taliban attacks mainly in FATA near Peshawar, distant from proposed IFA locations
propositions.quote: The evidence that the Taliban has carried out attacks... mainly in the region previously known as the FATA, close to the Appellant's home in Peshawar region, and in other regions distant from the proposed IFA locations.

propositions.text: Hyderabad, Multan, Lahore are large urban centers providing anonymity
propositions.quote: The proposed IFA in Hyderabad (a city of over 3 million people), Multan (a city of 1.3 million) or Lahore, (a city of 8.741 million people), which all qualify as a "large urban center" that would provide a "degree of anonymity" as stated in the U.K. Home Office document.

propositions.text: Targeting appellant in these cities would require a coordinated, networked entity which TTP lacks
propositions.quote: it would take a significantly coordinated, networked and organized entity to target the Appellant in Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore. The documentary evidence does not support the notion that the TTP has that organizational ability.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds no evidence TTP can track appellant to IFA cities; these cities offer anonymity; TTP lacks coordination to target him there.

propositions.text: To target appellant in IFA cities, TTP must learn of return, relocation, and whereabouts
propositions.quote: the TTP would be required to: 1.) Learn the Appellant has returned to Pakistan; 2.) Learn the Appellant has relocated to Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore; and 3.) Determine the whereabouts of the Appellant in Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds TTP would need to learn appellant's return, relocation, and location to target him in IFA cities.

propositions.text: If TTP had strength to track appellant, objective evidence would support this
propositions.quote: The RAD finds it reasonable to expect that if an organization was of sufficient strength and reach to be able to learn of a person's return to Pakistan or their presence in any city in Pakistan, there would be objective country condition evidence to support this.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds no objective evidence supports TTP's capacity to track appellant's movements in Pakistan.

propositions.text: Appellant was targeted by TTP individuals but no credible evidence TTP can track him after return
propositions.quote: as much as it accepts that the Appellant was targeted by individuals who identified themselves as members of the TTP, there is not sufficient credible evidence to establish that they have the operational capacity or geographic reach to learn of the Appellant's return to Pakistan upon arrival at a regular port of entry to the country, or trace the Appellant's movements within Pakistan.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD accepts appellant was targeted by TTP individuals but finds no credible evidence TTP can track him after return.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence does not support that the TTP has that ability in Pakistan
propositions.quote: The RAD finds the documentary evidence does not support that the TTP has that ability in Pakistan.

propositions.text: RAD supports the findings of the RPD in this instance
propositions.quote: The RAD supports the findings of the RPD in this instance.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds documentary evidence does not support TTP's ability in Pakistan and supports the RPD's findings.

propositions.text: Appellant testified as member of XXXX XXXX where he lived
propositions.quote: The RAD notes the Appellant has testified that he was a member of the XXXX XXXX where he lived.

propositions.text: RPD misstated Appellant's risk due to his profile as sub-leader of volunteers
propositions.quote: The RAD has considered the Appellant's submission that the RPD misstated the Appellant's risk due to his profile as a sub-leader of volunteers (as described in his BOC narrative).

propositions.text: Appellant did not occupy a high profile position in his committee
propositions.quote: The RAD has reviewed the Appellant's testimony in respect of his activities and it has previously found that the Appellant did not occupy a high profile position in his committee.

propositions.text: Appellant lived 3-4 months in XXXX area without Taliban seeking him out
propositions.quote: The RAD further considered that the Appellant had resided in the XXXX area of XXXX for three to four months without the Taliban seeking him out.

propositions.text: It is highly unlikely Appellant would be personally targeted by Taliban in other areas in Pakistan
propositions.quote: Therefore, the RAD finds the Appellant's it highly unlikely the Appellant would be personally targeted by the Taliban in other areas in Pakistan.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD notes appellant's testimony, considers his argument about risk, finds he had no high profile role and lived safely in XXXX area, so unlikely to be targeted elsewhere.

propositions.text: RPD ignored documentary evidence of risk to Appellant as local peace committee member
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that the RPD ignored the documentary evidence of the risk to the Appellant as a member of his local peace committee.

propositions.text: RAD reviewed specific documentary evidence addressed by Appellant and IRB country documents
propositions.quote: the RAD has reviewed the specific documentary evidence addressed by the Appellant30 as well as the IRB country documents to conduct its own assessment.

propositions.text: UK Home Office document describes Taliban's primary targets and areas of operation
propositions.quote: The RAD notes the UK Home Office document describes the profile of individuals sought by the Taliban and the principle areas where this occurs: Primary targets include political and/or tribal leaders, security forces and minority religious groups.

propositions.text: Ordinary Pakistanis opposing Taliban or not following sharia law also subjected to violence
propositions.quote: However, ordinary Pakistanis, including students and those perceived to be opposing the Taliban and other militant groups or not following sharia law, have also been subjected to violence by these groups.

propositions.text: Risk highest in areas where armed anti-government groups operate or control
propositions.quote: The risk will be highest in areas where those armed anti-government groups are operating or have control.

propositions.text: Main areas: Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, FATA, Baluchistan; Taliban have reach outside these areas
propositions.quote: Those main areas are: * Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (formerly known as North West Frontier Province), * The semi-autonomous Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA) that have a strong Taliban presence; and * Baluchistan, where separatists are seeking greater political autonomy and control over local mineral resources. The Pakistani Taliban and other militant groups do however have reach outside of those areas.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant argues RPD ignored risk evidence; RAD reviews evidence including UK Home Office document describing Taliban targets and areas of operation.

propositions.text: Documents describe attacks in Peshawar region between March 2011 and May 2013
propositions.quote: The RAD finds the documents addressed by the Appellant describe attacks within the Peshawar region during a period between March 2011 and May 2013.

propositions.text: Two episodes involved roadside IEDs not targeting one individual
propositions.quote: at least two of the episodes involved roadside IEDs (Improvised Explosive Devices) which were not specifically targeting one individual.

propositions.text: One targeted individual had history of conflict with Taliban linked to deaths of nine militants
propositions.quote: Another individual described in one of the articles as being targeted, had a long history of conflict with the Taliban and was linked to the deaths of nine Taliban militants in 2009.

propositions.text: Peace Committee in that area being disbanded due to risk to participants
propositions.quote: The RAD further notes an additional article indicates the Peace Committee in that area is being disbanded because of the risk involved to its participants.

propositions.text: Articles allege Taliban responsible but no specific organization claimed responsibility
propositions.quote: The RAD also finds that the articles allege the Taliban are responsible for these events, but a number of the articles clearly note that no specific organization has claimed responsibility for the events.

paragraphs.summary: RAD finds documents describe attacks in Peshawar region, some not targeting individuals, Peace Committee disbanded due to risk, Taliban alleged but no claims of responsibility.

propositions.text: Evidence confirms risk to high profile individuals in Peshawar during article period
propositions.quote: The RAD finds the evidence does confirm the risk to individuals, especially those of a high profile, during the time period of the articles, in the Peshawar area.

propositions.text: No persuasive evidence Taliban targeted XXXX XXXX outside immediate Peshawar region
propositions.quote: The RAD having reviewed all of the documentary evidence available finds there is no persuasive evidence that the Taliban have conducted any operations associated with the targeting of XXXX XXXX outside of the immediate Peshawar region.

paragraphs.summary: RAD finds risk confirmed for high profile individuals in Peshawar but no evidence Taliban targeted XXXX XXXX outside Peshawar.

propositions.text: Appellant addressed articles in Memorandum alleging RPD ignored them
propositions.quote: The RAD notes the Appellant has also addressed a number of articles31 in the Memorandum that it alleges the RPD ignored in the Appellant's post hearing submissions.

propositions.text: RAD reviewed these articles and finds they address non-targeted suicide attacks in Multan and Lahore linked to Taliban factions
propositions.quote: The RAD has reviewed these articles and finds they address non-targeted suicide attacks in locations in Multan and Lahore allegedly associated with factions of the Taliban.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant alleges RPD ignored articles; RAD reviews and finds they describe non-targeted suicide attacks in Multan and Lahore linked to Taliban factions.

propositions.text: 4 of 5 articles confirm police or authorities arrested or stopped Taliban members in terrorism activities
propositions.quote: The RAD finds it of interest that 4 of 5 articles confirmed the action of the police or the authorities in arresting, detaining or stopping Taliban members involved in various terrorism related activities.

propositions.text: A sixth article references authorities protecting jail superintendent from Taliban militants
propositions.quote: A sixth article references the authorities intercepting a telephone call and attempting to protect a jail superintendent in Hyderabad from Taliban militants.

propositions.text: Articles indicate limited non-targeted Taliban activity in IFA areas and authorities have some success addressing terrorism
propositions.quote: The RAD finds these articles indicate limited non-targeted activity by Taliban factions in the areas of the IFA, but more importantly the RAD finds they demonstrate that Pakistani authorities have attempted with some success to address terrorism related issues in these areas.

paragraphs.summary: RAD finds articles show police arrested Taliban members and limited Taliban activity in IFA areas; authorities have some success addressing terrorism.

propositions.text: Evidence does not indicate Taliban targeted individuals like Appellant or can search for him outside Peshawar region
propositions.quote: The RAD further finds that this evidence does not indicate that the Taliban has targeted specific individuals with a profile such as the Appellant, nor does it confirm that the Taliban the willingness or ability to search for the Appellant outside of XXXX in the Peshawar region.

paragraphs.summary: RAD finds evidence does not show Taliban targeted individuals like Appellant or can search for him outside Peshawar.

propositions.text: Appellant may have been targeted by TTP individuals in home village but no credible evidence TTP can track him in Pakistan
propositions.quote: The RAD has reviewed the submissions of the Appellant, the available documentary evidence, and finds that as much as the Appellant may have been targeted by individuals in his home village who identified themselves as members of the TTP, there is not sufficient credible evidence to establish that they have the operational capacity or geographic reach to learn of the Appellant's return to Pakistan upon arrival at a regular port of entry to the country, or trace the Appellant's movements within Pakistan.

paragraphs.summary: RAD finds no credible evidence TTP can track Appellant in Pakistan despite possible targeting in home village.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence does not support TTP has ability in Pakistan; RAD agrees with RPD findings
propositions.quote: The RAD has previously discussed that the documentary evidence does not support that the TTP has that ability in Pakistan. The RAD agrees with the findings of the RPD in this instance.

paragraphs.summary: RAD agrees with RPD that documentary evidence does not support TTP's ability in Pakistan.

propositions.text: No persuasive evidence TTP in XXXX searched for Appellant since 2014 or can locate him elsewhere in Pakistan
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that no persuasive evidence was advanced to confirm that the TTP in XXXX have searched for the Appellant in Pakistan since he left the area in XXXX 2014. As well the RAD notes no evidence was presented to the RPD or RAD to suggest that the alleged agent of persecution has the willingness or ability to search for the Appellant elsewhere in the country.

propositions.text: Appellant failed to provide persuasive evidence to corroborate speculation TTP can locate him elsewhere
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the Appellant has not provided sufficient persuasive evidence to corroborate his speculation that the individuals from the TTP in XXXX who sent letters to him and sought him, have the ability to locate him elsewhere in Pakistan.

propositions.text: Problem faced by Appellant is limited and local; Appellant's argument fails
propositions.quote: As such, the RAD finds the problem faced by the Appellant is limited and local in nature. The RAD finds the Appellant's argument must fail.

paragraphs.summary: RAD finds no evidence TTP searched for Appellant since 2014 or can locate him elsewhere; problem is local and argument fails.

propositions.text: Proposed IFAs Hyderabad, Multan, Lahore qualify as large urban centers
propositions.quote: The RAD has previously discussed that the proposed IFA in Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore are centres which qualify as a "large urban centers".

propositions.text: RPD questioned Appellant about ability to reside in these cities; Appellant said no safe place in Pakistan
propositions.quote: The RAD notes the RPD questioned the Appellant about his ability to reside in Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore and he testified that his only concern was that there is no safe place in Pakistan.

propositions.text: Appellant testified Taliban could track him due to wide network including government and police
propositions.quote: He testified that the Taliban could track him down because they have a wide network including connections in government and the police.

paragraphs.summary: RAD notes proposed IFAs are large urban centers; Appellant testified Taliban could track him due to wide network.

propositions.text: Appellant provided no credible evidence how Taliban could track him in IFAs
propositions.quote: The RAD notes the Appellant provided no credible testimony or evidence as to how this might occur.

propositions.text: Country documents and Appellant's evidence do not corroborate allegations
propositions.quote: The RAD has considered that a review of the RPD country condition documents and the Appellant's documentary evidence do not corroborate the Appellant's allegations.

propositions.text: No serious possibility Appellant would face persecution by TTP in Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore
propositions.quote: The RAD finds upon its review of the evidence there is not a serious possibility that the Appellant would face persecution at the hands of members of the TTP in Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore.

paragraphs.summary: RAD finds no credible evidence Taliban could track Appellant in IFAs and no serious possibility of persecution there.

propositions.text: Appellant has grade eight education, international travel experience, familiarity with asylum procedures, diploma, and language skills
propositions.quote: The RAD notes the Appellant has a grade eight education, he is an experienced international traveller and has resided in a number of locations. He has testified to being familiar with asylum procedures in the United States and Canada. In addition he has a diploma in XXXX XXXX and speaks Urdu, Pashto and some English.

propositions.text: No evidence Appellant showed circumstances making Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore unreasonable IFAs
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the Appellant has not adduced any evidence to confirm that there are any circumstances or conditions which would make Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore an unreasonable IFA.

paragraphs.summary: RAD notes Appellant's education and experience and finds no evidence these cities are unreasonable IFAs for him.

propositions.text: Appellant's argument insufficient to justify failure to attempt relocation within home country
propositions.quote: The RAD does not find the Appellant's argument sufficient to justify his failure to attempt relocation within his home country.

paragraphs.summary: RAD finds Appellant's argument insufficient to justify failure to attempt relocation within Pakistan.

propositions.text: Test for reasonableness of IFA is whether it would be unduly harsh to expect relocation before seeking status abroad
propositions.quote: The test for reasonableness is whether it would be unduly harsh to expect the Appellant to move to another, less hostile part of the country before seeking status abroad as per Thirunavukkarasu.

propositions.text: Evaluation requires conditions in IFA and Appellant's circumstances; high threshold for unreasonableness
propositions.quote: This requires an evaluation of the conditions in the IFA as well as the Appellant or similarly situated persons. Thirunavukkarasu sets a very high threshold for what makes an IFA unreasonable in all the circumstances.

propositions.text: Hardship of dislocation and relocation is not undue hardship making IFA unreasonable
propositions.quote: The hardship associated with dislocation and relocation is not the kind of undue hardship that renders an IFA unreasonable.

propositions.text: Dislike of weather, lack of friends or work is insufficient to make IFA unreasonable
propositions.quote: Additionally, it is not enough for the Appellant to say that he or she does not like the weather there, or that he or she has no friends or relatives there, or that he or she may not be able to find suitable work.

paragraphs.summary: The test for IFA reasonableness requires high threshold; hardship of relocation is not undue hardship; dislike of weather or lack of friends insufficient.

propositions.text: On balance of probabilities, no serious social, economic or other barriers to Appellant relocating to Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore
propositions.quote: The RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that there are no serious social, economic or other barriers to the Appellant relocating to Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore.

propositions.text: Appellant would not suffer undue hardship relocating to these cities
propositions.quote: The RAD finds after a full assessment of the evidence that the Appellant would not suffer from undue hardship in relocating to Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore.

paragraphs.summary: RAD finds no serious barriers or undue hardship for Appellant relocating to Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore.

propositions.text: RAD agrees with RPD that it would not be unreasonable for Appellant to seek refuge in Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore
propositions.quote: The RAD, therefore, agrees with the finding of the RPD and finds that it would not be unreasonable, in all the circumstances, including those particular to the Appellant, for him to seek refuge there.

paragraphs.summary: RAD agrees with RPD that seeking refuge in Hyderabad, Multan or Lahore would not be unreasonable for Appellant.

propositions.text: Appellant has not satisfied burden to establish serious possibility of persecution or risk to life or cruel treatment
propositions.quote: Accordingly, the RAD finds that the Appellant has not satisfied his burden of establishing that there is a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground or that, on a balance of probabilities, he would be personally subjected to a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture.

paragraphs.summary: RAD finds Appellant failed to prove serious possibility of persecution or risk to life or cruel treatment.

propositions.text: Pursuant to IRPA s.111(1)(a), RAD confirms RPD decision and dismisses appeal
propositions.quote: Pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD and dismisses the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: RAD confirms RPD decision and dismisses appeal under IRPA s.111(1)(a).
